Author: @Davivd2
Content:
The right to a speedy trial is violated here. But there is also something shady going on with that. If you are on probation, and your PO violates you, there really isn't a lengthy court process. I've never been arrested, but I've known people who have violated probation and the PO just goes in to see the judge, says the defendant violated in this way, and The defendant goes back to jail to serve out the remainder of their sentence on their original charge. So this lengthy trial is very suspicious. All that should have happened is that the PO said that he used the software that he used, it circumvented his monitoring, and the judge should have shipped him off on his sentence.

There is a scenario where the defendant himself is drawing this out in court. If he has his lawyer contesting every little detail, throwing up every delay possible. Asking for extensions to review evidence, then it's possible that this could have dragged on and on, far longer than it needed to be. The reason to do this is that in some states, they give you 2x credit time served for pre sentencing detention. If Rockenhaus knew that he was going to to back to jail, and was facing something like a 7 year sentence, he's knocked 3 years off of that with 2x time served in detention. The judge may eventually find him guilty and release him on time served with the 2x clause.

What triggers a red flag for me was that the wife was vague and not forthcoming about his original crime. She omitted her husbands complicity and painted her self as the victim. They may very well be the victims here but their actions in the matter don't exactly illicit feelings of trust from me. Common sense should have told him not to get involved with obfuscation software like TOR while being monitored to begin with. That's SUS.
